lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Why are you crying, Tantalus? And why stand there in the lake making a tragedy of yourself?

lines.speaker: Tantalus
lines.text: Because, Menippus, I am dying of thirst.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Are you really that lazy? Bend down and drink. Or, for Zeus' sake, scoop some up in your hand.

lines.speaker: Tantalus
lines.text: No use. If I bend down, the water runs away the moment it notices me coming. And if I do manage to scoop some up and bring it to my mouth, I barely wet the edge of my lip before it slips through my fingers—somehow—and leaves my hand dry again.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: That is a very special problem, Tantalus. But tell me: what do you need a drink for? You have no body. That is buried somewhere in Lydia—the part of you that could get hungry and thirsty. You are the soul. How can you still be thirsty, or drink?

lines.speaker: Tantalus
lines.text: That is the punishment: the soul thirsts as if it were a body.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: All right, we will accept that, since you say thirst is your sentence. But what is the actual danger? Are you afraid you will die from lack of drink? I do not see another Hades after this one, or a death from here into some further establishment.

lines.speaker: Tantalus
lines.text: You are right. Still, this too is part of the sentence: wanting to drink when I have no need to.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Nonsense, Tantalus. In fact you do seem to need a drink—undiluted hellebore, by Zeus. You have the opposite complaint from people bitten by mad dogs: you are afraid not of water, but of thirst.

lines.speaker: Tantalus
lines.text: I would not refuse the hellebore either, Menippus, if only I could get it.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Take heart, Tantalus. Neither you nor any other corpse is going to drink; it is impossible. Though, to be fair, not everyone is thirsty by court order, with the water personally refusing to cooperate.
